Chess Tournament

Game StrategyAlgebraLogic
Game: Three chess players take turns: the winner of each game plays the one who sat out, and the first to win two games takes the series.
How to play: Slide p, q and r to change how often the stronger player wins. Read the table or the bars to see who is likely to win, then pick a first game with the buttons or the arrow keys.

The bars show B's row of the table. B chooses which game comes first.

Look for the math

Three players, one series, and a choice that feels backwards. Before a single game is played, how likely is each player to be the one who collects two wins first? The table answers that question for every starting pair.

Following an event tree

There are no draws, and the winner of a game plays the player who sat it out. Someone reaches two wins in at most four games, so the whole series is a small event tree: follow a branch, multiply the chances along it, and add the branches that end the same way. We assume the games are independent events, just as the applet's page does. Starting A vs B, B vs C, or A vs C gives three different trees and the three columns of the table.

B's two chances

Write p for A's chance against B, q for B's chance against C, and r for A's chance against C. Adding the branches gives the two chances the page asks us to compare:

PAB = p(1 − r)q(1 − p) + (1 − p)q + (1 − p)(1 − q)r(1 − p)
PBC = q(1 − p) + qp(1 − r)q + (1 − q)r(1 − p)q

The logic test checked both formulas, and a separate walk of every branch of the game tree, at all 51 × 51 × 51 = 132,651 settings of the three sliders. They agree, and each column of the table adds to 1.

Why starting against C is best

The term (1 − p)q appears in both chances and cancels. What is left factors neatly:

PBC − PAB = [pq(1 − r) + (1 − p)(1 − q)r] (p + q − 1)

Because both p and q exceed 0.5, the last bracket is positive, so B does at least as well by starting against the weak C. The page says "always <", but that is a little too strong: there are 49 boundary settings with q = r = 1 where the two chances are exactly equal. The test also confirms the page's note that r > p is not needed for the comparison; without it the only ties are at p = r = 1. A full search shows B vs C is never worse than either other start.

A typo in the old applet

The original bytecode computes one branch of PAB with p where the game tree needs 1 − p. At the starting values this makes its AB column add to 1.0135 instead of 1. This page follows the probability formula printed on cut-the-knot, which the branch-by-branch count confirms; the test pins the old applet's exact error so the difference is not hidden. It is a small game theory puzzle: B gets to choose the first pairing, and the choice matters.

Try q = 1.00 and r = 1.00: A always beats C and B always beats C, so starting A vs B and starting B vs C give B exactly the same chance. Can you see why from the tree?

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
